paper_context.research_question: Can a novel, fully non-monotonic transition system based on the non-projective Covington algorithm, trained with approximate dynamic oracles, achieve superior dependency parsing accuracy compared to its monotonic counterpart, especially for unrestricted non-projective parsing?
main_claims: A novel, fully non-monotonic transition system based on the non-projective Covington algorithm is proposed, which can repair previous erroneous attachments regardless of direction and uses an exclusively non-monotonic oracle.

Several non-monotonic variants of a dynamic oracle for the Covington parser are developed, utilizing tight, efficiently-computable approximations of the loss due to the complexity of exact calculation in a non-monotonic and non-projective scenario.
The presented system is the first non-monotonic parser capable of producing non-projective dependency analyses.

Experimental results on CoNLL-X and CoNLL-XI datasets demonstrate that the non-monotonic dynamic oracle outperforms the monotonic version in the majority of languages, with an average improvement of 0.32 UAS.

The approximate dynamic oracles are empirically shown to be very tight approximations of the real loss (relative errors below 0.8%) and are sufficient for achieving better accuracy than the exact monotonic oracle.
The non-monotonic system, particularly with the lower bound loss expression, can be faster than the monotonic approach as it avoids cycle computation.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a novel, fully non-monotonic transition system for dependency parsing, built upon the non-projective Covington algorithm and trained with approximate dynamic oracles. The logical flow begins by establishing the limitations of existing monotonic and restricted non-monotonic parsers, particularly their inability to handle full error repair and non-projectivity simultaneously. It then introduces the Covington parser as a suitable foundation due to its inherent flexibility. The core contribution is the design of a non-monotonic Covington system with a novel constraint enforcement mechanism and the development of approximate dynamic oracles to manage the complexity of exact loss calculation. The paper proceeds to empirically validate the tightness of these approximations and demonstrates the superior parsing accuracy and, in some cases, efficiency of the non-monotonic system over its monotonic counterpart. The argument is generally well-structured, moving from problem identification to proposed solution, detailed mechanism, and empirical validation. However, some aspects of the empirical findings, particularly the performance of the 'farthest' loss approximation, introduce a minor logical discontinuity that the paper addresses with a hypothesis rather than a definitive explanation.
logical_argument_graph: Existing greedy transition-based parsers suffer from error propagation and permanent errors due to monotonicity (Introduction).
Prior non-monotonic approaches (e.g., Honnibal et al., Honnibal and Johnson) are restricted in their repair capabilities and limited to projective trees (Introduction).
The non-projective Covington transition system is inherently less rigid and allows revisiting words, making it a better candidate for full non-monotonicity (C8, A1).
Therefore, a novel, fully non-monotonic transition system based on the non-projective Covington algorithm is proposed (C1).
This system is designed to repair previous erroneous attachments regardless of direction and uses an exclusively non-monotonic oracle (C1, C7).
This proposed system is claimed to be the first non-monotonic parser capable of producing non-projective dependency analyses (C2).

Due to the complexity of exact loss calculation in a non-monotonic and non-projective scenario, several non-monotonic variants of a dynamic oracle are developed using tight, efficiently-computable approximations of the loss (C3).
These approximate dynamic oracles are empirically shown to be very tight approximations of the real loss (C5).
Experimental results demonstrate that the non-monotonic dynamic oracle outperforms the monotonic version in the majority of languages (C4).

Specifically, the loss expression |U(c, tG)| + nc(A ∪ I(c, tG)) (the 'upper bound'), despite being empirically 'farthest' from the real loss, obtains greater accuracy on average than other non-monotonic loss expressions (C10).
The non-monotonic dynamic oracle with the best loss expression also achieves a greater average improvement over the static version compared to the monotonic oracle (C11).
Furthermore, the non-monotonic system, particularly with the lower bound loss expression, can be faster than the monotonic approach as it avoids cycle computation (C6).

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This work is directly comparable as it introduced restricted non-monotonicity to arc-eager dependency parsing. The current paper differentiates itself by proposing *full* non-monotonicity and applying it to the non-projective Covington system, addressing limitations of the arc-eager approach (e.g., inability to repair leftward arcs, projective only).

An extension of Honnibal et al. (2013), this work also explored restricted non-monotonicity in arc-eager systems. The current paper builds upon and explicitly contrasts with this work by offering a fully non-monotonic, non-projective solution.

This paper defines the monotonic dynamic oracle for the non-projective Covington parser, serving as the direct baseline and a foundational component that the current work modifies and extends to be non-monotonic and approximate.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper's core contribution—a fully non-monotonic transition system for unrestricted non-projective parsing with approximate dynamic oracles—demonstrates significant conceptual novelty. The lack of direct analogs in the retrieved literature, beyond prior work on *restricted* non-monotonicity, supports this. The methodological soundness of the approximate oracles and their empirical validation are distinct from this inherent novelty; the paper successfully addresses the validity of its approximations as a practical necessity.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: The approximate dynamic oracles maintain their empirically demonstrated tightness and effectiveness across a broader range of linguistic phenomena, sentence lengths, and parsing complexities than evaluated in the initial 100,000 transitions.

Future research could demonstrate that the 'farthest' performing oracle (C10) is not merely a statistical artifact but genuinely provides a more robust or learnable signal for statistical models, perhaps by simplifying the learning task in complex non-monotonic scenarios.

The system's performance generalizes well to languages with diverse typological characteristics, and any observed performance drops (e.g., in Basque) can be systematically addressed through targeted feature engineering or model adaptations.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a novel, fully non-monotonic transition system for unrestricted non-projective dependency parsing, building upon the Covington algorithm. A key aspect is the development of approximate dynamic oracles, necessitated by the computational intractability of exact loss calculation in this complex non-monotonic and non-projective setting. The system allows for the repair of previously erroneous attachments regardless of arc direction and operates with an exclusively non-monotonic oracle. Empirical results on CoNLL-X and CoNLL-XI datasets indicate that this non-monotonic approach generally outperforms its monotonic counterpart in parsing accuracy (UAS), with an average improvement of 0.32 UAS. The approximate oracles are empirically demonstrated to be very tight approximations of the real loss. Furthermore, the lower bound loss expression is highlighted for its computational efficiency, making the non-monotonic system faster than the monotonic one.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a significant incremental advancement in transition-based dependency parsing by introducing a novel, fully non-monotonic transition system based on the non-projective Covington algorithm. This extends prior work on restricted non-monotonicity (Honnibal et al., 2013; Honnibal and Johnson, 2015) by enabling repair of any erroneous attachment, regardless of direction, and applying it to non-projective structures, a combination previously unexplored. A key contribution is the development of approximate dynamic oracles to train this complex system, addressing the intractability of exact loss calculation in a non-monotonic, non-projective setting. The empirical evaluation demonstrates that these approximate non-monotonic oracles generally outperform their monotonic counterpart, with an average UAS improvement of 0.32, validating the practical utility of the proposed extensions. The work also highlights an interesting finding where a 'farthest' approximation of the loss yields better practical accuracy, suggesting nuanced learning dynamics in such systems.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Greedy transition-based parsers suffer from error propagation; existing non-monotonic systems are restricted (only certain repairs, projective trees) and often use mixed monotonic/non-monotonic oracles (Introduction, lines 101-169).

Hypothesis: A fully non-monotonic system, especially one based on the flexible Covington parser, can offer superior repair capabilities and thus better accuracy for unrestricted non-projective parsing (Introduction, lines 170-182, Assumption A1).

Solution 1 (System Design): Propose a novel, fully non-monotonic Covington transition system that allows all arc transitions to repair previous attachments and enforces single-head/acyclicity by immediately removing offending arcs (Claim C1, C7, Section 3). This is claimed to be the first non-monotonic parser for non-projective analyses (Claim C2).
Problem (Oracle): Exact loss calculation for a fully non-monotonic and non-projective oracle is intractable (Section 4, lines 452-458).

Solution 2 (Oracle Design): Develop several non-monotonic variants of a dynamic oracle using tight, efficiently-computable approximations of the loss (Claim C3, Section 4). These include a lower bound, a closer upper bound (problematic cycles), and a general upper bound (all cycles).

Validation 1 (Oracle Tightness): Empirically evaluate the tightness of these approximate oracles against real loss via exhaustive search on a subset of transitions, showing relative errors below 0.8% for the lower and closer upper bounds (Claim C5, Section 5, Table 1).
Validation 2 (Parsing Accuracy): Conduct experiments on CoNLL-X/XI datasets comparing static, monotonic, and non-monotonic dynamic oracles (Section 6).

Result 1 (Superiority): The non-monotonic dynamic oracle (especially with the general upper bound loss) outperforms the monotonic version in most languages, with an average UAS improvement of 0.32 (Claim C4, Section 6, Table 3). It also shows greater improvement over the static oracle than the monotonic one (Claim C11).
Result 2 (Oracle Effectiveness): The approximate oracles are sufficient for achieving better accuracy than the exact monotonic oracle (Claim C4, Assumption A2).

Result 3 (Unexpected Oracle Performance): The loss expression that is empirically 'farthest' from the real loss (general upper bound) obtains greater accuracy on average (Claim C10, Section 6, lines 740-744).

Hypothesis (Learning Dynamics): This unexpected result suggests that statistical models may struggle to learn complex cycle-breaking scenarios, making a simpler, more conservative loss signal more effective (Assumption A3, Section 6, lines 750-756).

Result 4 (Efficiency): The non-monotonic system using the lower bound loss is the fastest option, even faster than the monotonic approach, as it avoids cycle computation (Claim C6, Section 4, lines 590-594).

Conclusion: The proposed fully non-monotonic Covington parser with approximate dynamic oracles is a novel and effective approach for unrestricted non-projective parsing, demonstrating improved accuracy and practical efficiency (Section 7).

concerns.description: The observation that the 'farthest' approximation of the real loss (the general upper bound) yields the best parsing accuracy (Claim C10), while the 'closer' upper bound does not, is counter-intuitive. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a conceptually novel, fully non-monotonic transition system for unrestricted non-projective dependency parsing, building upon the Covington algorithm. It departs significantly from prior work on non-monotonic parsing by allowing repairs of both leftward and rightward arcs and exclusively employing a non-monotonic dynamic oracle, rather than a monotonic fallback. A key innovation lies in the design of approximate dynamic oracles, necessitated by the computational intractability of exact loss calculation in this highly flexible, non-monotonic, and non-projective setting. The paper formalizes this new transition system and its associated approximate oracles, then empirically demonstrates that the non-monotonic approach, particularly with one of its approximate loss functions, generally outperforms its monotonic counterpart in parsing accuracy across multiple languages. The finding that a 'farthest' approximation of the loss performs best, coupled with the hypothesis that statistical models struggle to learn complex cycle-breaking scenarios, introduces a thought-provoking perspective on oracle design and model learnability in highly non-monotonic systems.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Traditional greedy transition-based parsers suffer from error propagation and cannot repair past mistakes. Existing non-monotonic parsers are limited (projective, restricted repairs, monotonic oracle fallback). Exact loss calculation for a fully non-monotonic, non-projective system is intractable.

Proposed Solution (System): Introduce a novel, fully non-monotonic transition system based on the non-projective Covington algorithm (C1). This system allows repair of any arc direction (left/right) and uses an exclusively non-monotonic oracle. It enforces single-head and acyclicity by immediately removing offending arcs, rather than forbidding transitions (C7), leveraging the Covington algorithm's inherent flexibility (A1).

Proposed Solution (Oracle): Develop approximate dynamic oracles for this system (C3). These oracles use efficiently-computable lower and upper bounds of the loss, as exact calculation is too complex. Three loss expressions are defined: a lower bound, a 'problematic cycles' upper bound (pc upper), and a general 'cycles' upper bound (upper).

Evaluation (Oracle Tightness): Empirically demonstrate that the approximate dynamic oracles are very tight approximations of the real loss (C5), with relative errors below 0.8% for the lower and pc upper bounds (A6).
Evaluation (Performance): Conduct experiments on CoNLL-X/XI datasets comparing static, monotonic dynamic, and non-monotonic dynamic oracles (with its three loss variants).

Result 1 (Accuracy): The non-monotonic dynamic oracle (specifically with the 'upper' loss expression) outperforms the monotonic version in most languages, with an average UAS improvement of 0.32 (C4).
Result 2 (Efficiency): The non-monotonic system using the lower bound loss is faster than the monotonic approach, as it avoids cycle computation (C6).

Result 3 (Oracle Effectiveness): The 'upper' loss expression, though empirically farther from the real loss than 'pc upper', yields better parsing accuracy (C10). This is hypothesized to be due to the difficulty for the statistical model to learn complex cycle-breaking scenarios (A3).

Result 4 (Overall Improvement): The non-monotonic dynamic oracle with the best loss expression achieves a greater average improvement over the static version (1.26 UAS) compared to the monotonic oracle (0.98 UAS) (C11).

Conclusion: The proposed fully non-monotonic system with approximate dynamic oracles offers a novel and effective approach to unrestricted non-projective dependency parsing, demonstrating superior accuracy and practical feasibility despite the inherent complexity of the problem.

This goes beyond previous limited non-monotonic approaches (e.g., Honnibal et al.) by allowing repairs of both leftward and rightward arcs and relying exclusively on a non-monotonic oracle. This represents a significant conceptual leap in transition-based parsing, pushing the boundaries of what is considered 'repairable' within the parsing process.

concerns.title: Counter-intuitive Oracle Performance and Learnability Hypothesis
concerns.description: The finding that the 'upper bound' loss expression, which is empirically farther from the real loss, performs better than the 'pc upper' bound (which is provably closer) is counter-intuitive and raises questions about the optimal learning signal. The hypothesis that statistical models struggle to learn complex cycle-breaking situations (A3) is plausible but remains an unproven assumption. This suggests a potential disconnect between theoretical loss approximation and practical model learnability, which is a novelty risk inherent in the disruptive approach.
evidence: C10: The loss expression |U(c, tG)| + nc(A ∪ I(c, tG)) (the 'upper bound') obtains greater accuracy on average than the other two non-monotonic loss expressions, including the one empirically closer to the real loss.

A3: Even if an oracle with exact loss were feasible, it would not provide practical improvements over the approximate oracles, because it appears difficult for a statistical model to learn the complex situations where replacing a wrong arc indirectly helps by breaking prospective cycles.

Section 6 (lines 740-756): 'The loss expression |U(c, tG)| + nc(A ∪ I(c, tG)) obtains greater accuracy on average than the other two loss expressions, including the more adjusted upper bound that is provably closer to the real loss. This could be explained by the fact that identifying problematic cycles is a difficult task to learn for the parser, and for this reason a more straightforward approach, which tries to avoid all kinds of cycles (regardless of whether they will cost gold arcs or not), can perform better. This also leads us to hypothesize that, even if it were feasible to build an oracle with the exact loss, it would not provide practical improvements over these approximate oracles; as it appears difficult for a statistical model to learn the situations where replacing a wrong arc with another indirectly helps due to breaking prospective cycles.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: While the hypothesis is interesting, further analysis or theoretical grounding on the learnability aspects of different loss signals in highly non-monotonic settings would strengthen this claim. Exploring alternative learning algorithms or model architectures that might better leverage the 'closer' approximations could also be valuable.

While this might be a practical necessity due to computational complexity, it introduces an operational assumption that the behavior of these bounds remains consistent throughout the entire parsing process and for longer sentences. Deviations in later stages or for more complex configurations could impact the oracle's effectiveness.

If feasible, a qualitative analysis of loss bound behavior on a small, diverse set of longer or more complex sentences could provide additional confidence, even if full quantitative evaluation is prohibitive.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a novel, fully non-monotonic transition system for non-projective dependency parsing, building upon the Covington algorithm and employing approximate dynamic oracles. The core claims regarding the system's design, its ability to repair errors regardless of direction, and its exclusive use of a non-monotonic oracle (C1, C7) are well-supported by the formal descriptions and architectural details provided in the manuscript. The empirical claims of superior parsing accuracy over the monotonic version (C4, C11) and the tightness of the approximate oracles (C5) are strongly substantiated by the experimental results presented in tables and text. The claim of being the 'first' non-monotonic parser for non-projective analyses (C2) is explicitly qualified by the authors, indicating a reasonable level of self-awareness regarding its novelty. A notable finding is that the 'farthest' approximate loss expression empirically yields the best parsing accuracy (C10), which is an interesting, albeit counter-intuitive, result that the authors address with a plausible hypothesis (A3). However, the strong empirical claim about the lower bound oracle's superior efficiency (C6) is stated without direct runtime measurements, making it partially supported by theoretical argument rather than direct empirical evidence. The evaluation of loss bound tightness (C5) is limited to the first 100,000 transitions (A6), which might not fully generalize to the entire parsing process. Overall, the paper presents a coherent and largely evidence-backed argument for its proposed system, with identified uncertainties and limitations openly acknowledged or reasonably hypothesized.

Traditionally, the negation word is determined from a small hand- 727 Kiritchenko, Zhu, & Mohammad crafted list (Taboada et al., 2011). The scope of negation is often assumed to begin from the word following the negation word until the next punctuation mark or the end of the sentence (Polanyi & Zaenen, 2004; Kennedy & Inkpen, 2005). More sophisticated methods to detect the scope of negation through semantic parsing have also been proposed (Li, Zhou, Wang, & Zhu, 2010). A common way to capture the impact of negation is to reverse the polarities of the sentiment words in the scope of negation. Taboada et al. (2011) proposed to shift the sentiment score of a term in a negated context towards the opposite polarity by a ﬁxed amount. However, in their experiments the shift-score model did not agree with human judgment in many cases, especially for negated negative terms. More complex approaches, such as recursive deep models, address negation through semantic composition (Socher, Huval, Manning, & Ng, 2012; Socher et al., 2013). Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
